sections.name: Unreal Engine 5 Deep Dive
sections.explanation_simple: Unreal Engine 5 is like having a Hollywood movie studio on your computer - for free. It's the engine behind Fortnite, Gears of War, Hellblade 2, and Black Myth: Wukong. What makes UE5 special is Nanite (which lets you use movie-quality 3D models directly in your game without slowing down) and Lumen (which makes lighting look realistic automatically). You can build games using Blueprints (visual scripting - no coding needed) or C++ (for maximum power).
key_concepts: GameMode: The rules of your game (who wins, how scoring works)
GameState: Information every player needs to know (scores, time left)
PlayerController: Takes input and controls a Pawn (keyboard/mouse/controller)
Pawn/Character: The physical thing in the world (player model, enemy)
Actor: Everything in the game world (lights, cameras, props, characters)
Component: Attachable behavior (movement, sound, health)
Blueprint: Visual scripting - drag and connect nodes to make game logic
Nanite: Virtual geometry that auto-manages detail - use million-poly models directly
Lumen: Dynamic global illumination that bounces light realistically
World Partition: Automatically manages large open worlds

sections.name: Unity Engine Deep Dive
sections.explanation_simple: Unity is the world's most popular game engine - it powers games like Hollow Knight, Hearthstone, Genshin Impact, and Pokemon GO. Think of Unity as a giant Lego set for making games. Every piece in your game is a GameObject, and you give it abilities by adding Components (like a Renderer to make it visible, a Collider so things bump into it, a Rigidbody so it falls with gravity). You write C# scripts to create custom Components. Unity is great for 2D, 3D, mobile, and console games alike.
key_concepts: GameObject: Everything in your scene (empty container)
Component: A piece of functionality attached to a GameObject
Transform: Position, rotation, and scale (every object has one)
MonoBehaviour: The base class for all C# scripts
Prefabs: Reusable object templates (like blueprints)
Scenes: Containers for game levels/menus
Physics: Rigidbody + Collider = things that bump and fall
URP: Universal Render Pipeline (fast, mobile-friendly)
HDRP: High Definition Render Pipeline (beautiful, high-end)
Animator: Controls animation blending with state machines

sections.name: Godot Engine
sections.explanation_simple: Godot is the indie darling of game engines - it's completely free and open source (no royalties, no fees, ever). It uses a unique scene system where everything is a tree of nodes. Every node does one thing: a Sprite2D shows a picture, a CollisionShape2D handles physics, an AudioStreamPlayer plays sounds. You combine nodes into scenes, then you can put those scenes inside other scenes (like Russian nesting dolls). Godot uses GDScript (Python-like) or C# for scripting.
key_concepts: Nodes: Smallest building block (Sprite2D, Label, CollisionShape2D)
Scene: A collection of nodes saved as a file (a level, a player, a menu)
Scene tree: The hierarchy of all active nodes
Signals: Events that nodes emit (button pressed, timer finished)
GDScript: Python-like scripting language built for Godot
Groups: Tags to organize nodes (all enemies, all pickups)
@export: Makes variables editable in the inspector
AnimationPlayer: Node for animating properties
TileMap: For building tile-based levels

sections.name: Other Major Engines Overview
sections.explanation_simple: Besides Unity, Unreal, and Godot, there are many specialized engines. Some are used by specific game studios (like the RAGE engine that Rockstar uses for GTA), others are open-source alternatives. Understanding them helps you choose the right tool for your project.
key_concepts: CryEngine: Known for amazing graphics (Crysis), still used for some AAA titles
Frostbite: EA's engine (Battlefield, FIFA) - strong in destruction physics and large maps
id Tech: The engine behind DOOM and Quake (pure speed, id Software)
Source 2: Valve's engine (Dota 2, Half-Life: Alyx) - strong physics, VR support
RE Engine: Capcom's engine (Resident Evil 7/8/4R, Devil May Cry 5) - photorealistic horror
RAGE: Rockstar's engine (GTA V, RDR2) - massive open worlds, Euphoria physics
O3DE: Open 3D Engine (open-source, Linux Foundation) - AAA features, component-based

sections.name: Custom Engine Development
sections.explanation_simple: Sometimes you need to build your own engine. Maybe you want total control, maybe you're learning, or maybe none of the existing engines do what you need. Building an engine is like building a car from scratch instead of buying one - it's a LOT of work, but you'll understand every single piece. Most indie teams should use existing engines, but knowing how engines work internally makes you a better programmer in any engine.
key_concepts: Game loop: The heart that beats 60 times per second (input -> update -> render)
Entity-Component System: Efficient data-oriented entity management
Rendering pipeline: Takes 3D data and draws it on a 2D screen
Physics integration: Bullet, PhysX, or custom physics
Asset pipeline: Loading models, textures, sounds from files
Memory management: Custom allocators for game-specific patterns
Platform abstraction: One engine that runs on PC, console, mobile
Profiling: Measuring where time is spent to optimize
